title: Aurora Relay Station: Mastering Timeouts and Cancellation in Asyncio
details: Learner profile: comfortable with async def, await, coroutines, asyncio.Future, asyncio.gather; NOT yet exposed to queues or sync primitives (locks, events, etc.) - do not introduce these. Learning goal: next natural step in asyncio mastery - asyncio.wait_for() for timeouts and Task.cancel()/asyncio.CancelledError for cancellation, plus how the two interact (wait_for auto-cancels on timeout). Scope must stay narrow: only use asyncio.sleep, asyncio.create_task, asyncio.wait_for, Task.cancel(), asyncio.CancelledError, asyncio.TimeoutError, and asyncio.gather (already known). Do NOT introduce asyncio.wait(), as_completed, queues, locks, events, or semaphores. Story world: learner plays mission control operator at 'Aurora Relay Station,' a deep-space communications array tracking a small fleet of experimental probes (named Icarus-7, Vega-3, etc.) near the edge of the solar system. Probes occasionally go silent due to 'solar interference' (simulated via asyncio.sleep delays that may exceed acceptable wait times). Tone: friendly, approachable, light sci-fi flavor, plain-language analogies (e.g. wait_for = setting a kitchen timer while on hold; cancel = hanging up the phone). Problem set progresses: (1) intro/story only, (2) basic timeout handling with wait_for, (3) basic manual cancellation with Task.cancel(), (4) combining wait_for+cancel for fallback logic, (5) capstone combining per-task timeouts, overall mission timeout, and mass cancellation with gather. All simulated probe delays/timeouts should be small (0.1-3 seconds) for fast test runs.

parts.title: Welcome to Aurora Relay Station
parts.details: Pure narrative/orientation part, no coding or grading artifacts needed beyond a short conceptual explanation. Sets up: learner is new operator at Aurora Relay Station; fleet of probes (Icarus-7, Vega-3, others) transmit telemetry across vast distances; sometimes signals get lost or delayed indefinitely due to solar interference; operators historically just 'waited forever' which wasted power and time; new protocol requires using timeouts (asyncio.wait_for) and manual abort commands (Task.cancel()) to keep operations responsive. Preview the 4 upcoming hands-on modules in-story terms: taming a silent probe (timeouts), aborting a mission mid-transmission (cancellation), falling back to backup probes when primary is unresponsive (wait_for+cancel interaction), and running a full multi-probe contact protocol (capstone).
parts.description_agent_notes: Write warm, welcoming narrative intro; use plain-language analogy for timeout (kitchen timer / voicemail cutoff) and cancellation (hanging up a call) without code yet; briefly recap what learner already knows (async def, await, gather) and frame timeouts/cancellation as the natural next skill; end with a short roadmap of the 4 following stations/modules using the probe names introduced; keep tone light sci-fi, encouraging, beginner-friendly; no code snippets required, prose/point-form is fine.

parts.title: The Silent Probe - Taming Timeouts
parts.details: Introduce probe 'Icarus-7' whose response time varies due to interference. Functions to implement (fixed signatures for grading): async def ping_probe(probe_id: str, delay: float) -> str - awaits asyncio.sleep(delay) then returns f'Telemetry received from {probe_id}'. async def contact_probe(probe_id: str, delay: float, timeout: float) -> str - must wrap ping_probe call in asyncio.wait_for(..., timeout=timeout); on success return the telemetry string unchanged; on asyncio.TimeoutError catch it internally and return f'Lost contact with {probe_id} (timeout)'. No exception should ever propagate out of contact_probe. Edge cases to support: delay well below timeout (success), delay well above timeout (timeout message), and grader will avoid exact-equal boundary cases due to timing flakiness.
parts.description_agent_notes: Explain asyncio.wait_for(coro, timeout) syntax and asyncio.TimeoutError using the kitchen-timer/voicemail analogy from intro; tie explicitly to Icarus-7 sometimes being slow to respond due to interference; give a short illustrative example similar to the cows/spaceship style (e.g., 'If Icarus-7 takes 5 seconds to respond but we only wait 2, wait_for gives up and raises TimeoutError, which we catch to report lost contact'); mention default behavior that wait_for cancels the underlying coroutine automatically on timeout (planting the seed for Part 3/4) without going deep yet.
parts.coding_agent_notes: Provide starter file with: imports (asyncio), full working async def ping_probe as described (no TODO, given as helper), a stubbed async def contact_probe with TODO comments guiding the learner to wrap the ping_probe call in asyncio.wait_for inside a try/except asyncio.TimeoutError block; include a commented-out or __main__ demo block with 2-3 sample asyncio.run calls showing both a fast (success) and slow (timeout) probe scenario for local manual testing; keep code short and heavily commented for beginners; do not implement the TODO logic for the learner.

parts.title: Aborting the Mission - Task.cancel() Basics
parts.details: Introduce probe 'Vega-3' mid-transmission of a large data upload when a solar storm warning forces an abort. Functions to implement: async def upload_data(probe_id: str, chunks: int) -> str - loops chunk by chunk (for i in range(chunks): await asyncio.sleep(1) then print/log progress), and if asyncio.CancelledError is raised during a sleep, catch it, perform a short cleanup action (e.g. print/log 'Upload from {probe_id} aborted, saving partial data...'), then re-raise the CancelledError so the task correctly reports as cancelled. After the loop completes normally, return f'{probe_id} upload complete: {chunks} chunks sent'. async def abort_after(probe_id: str, chunks: int, abort_delay: float) -> str - creates the upload_data coroutine as a Task via asyncio.create_task, waits abort_delay seconds via asyncio.sleep, then calls task.cancel(); it must then await the task inside a try/except asyncio.CancelledError block and return an appropriate status string: if cancelled, return f'{probe_id} upload cancelled after partial transfer'; if the task had already finished before cancel() was called, return the task's original completion string instead (task.cancel() on an already-done task is a no-op, and awaiting it should just yield its result). Edge cases: abort_delay shorter than total upload time (should cancel mid-way) and abort_delay longer than total upload time (should complete normally, cancel() has no effect).
parts.description_agent_notes: Explain asyncio.create_task, that tasks run in the background once created, and that Task.cancel() requests cancellation which is delivered as an asyncio.CancelledError at the next await point inside the task; use the 'hanging up mid-call' analogy; explicitly teach the pattern: catch CancelledError, do cleanup, then re-raise so the task's cancelled state is preserved; connect back to Part 2's mention that wait_for does this automatically, whereas here we're doing it manually with an explicit abort command from mission control during the storm warning.
parts.coding_agent_notes: Provide starter file with: imports (asyncio), a stubbed async def upload_data with TODO markers for the loop, the try/except CancelledError cleanup block, and the re-raise; a stubbed async def abort_after with TODOs for creating the task, sleeping abort_delay, calling cancel(), and awaiting the task inside try/except CancelledError with the two required return-string branches; include comments warning learners not to forget to re-raise CancelledError in upload_data; include a small demo __main__ block with one short abort_delay and one long abort_delay example for manual sanity testing.

parts.title: Fallback Relay - When wait_for Meets cancel
parts.details: Story: primary probe Icarus-7 must relay urgent coordinates to avoid an incoming hazard; if it fails to respond within a short timeout, mission control must immediately fall back to backup probe Vega-3. Functions to implement: async def relay_message(probe_id: str, delay: float, message: str) -> str - awaits asyncio.sleep(delay) then returns f'{probe_id} relayed: {message}'. async def send_urgent_relay(primary_id: str, primary_delay: float, backup_id: str, backup_delay: float, message: str, primary_timeout: float, backup_timeout: float) -> str - first attempts asyncio.wait_for(relay_message(primary_id, primary_delay, message), timeout=primary_timeout); on success return that result immediately (backup must NOT be attempted). On asyncio.TimeoutError, catch it and then attempt asyncio.wait_for(relay_message(backup_id, backup_delay, message), timeout=backup_timeout); on success return that result; on a second asyncio.TimeoutError, catch it and return 'URGENT RELAY FAILED: both probes unresponsive'. Edge cases: primary succeeds (backup never runs - verify via side effect or timing), primary times out & backup succeeds, both time out.
parts.description_agent_notes: Reinforce that when asyncio.wait_for times out, it automatically cancels the coroutine/task it was given - explicitly narrate this as 'mission control doesn't need to manually hang up on Icarus-7, wait_for does it for us the instant the timer runs out' - directly connecting back to the manual Task.cancel() work in Part 3 so the learner sees both the manual and automatic cancellation paths; frame the fallback logic as a two-stage emergency protocol; keep explanation focused only on wait_for + its built-in cancellation, no new primitives.
parts.coding_agent_notes: Provide starter file with: imports (asyncio), given helper async def relay_message (fully implemented), a stubbed async def send_urgent_relay with TODO comments guiding: (1) wrap primary relay in asyncio.wait_for inside try, (2) on except asyncio.TimeoutError attempt backup relay in a nested asyncio.wait_for inside try, (3) on second except asyncio.TimeoutError return the failure string; include an optional comment showing that passing an already-created Task into wait_for behaves the same way as passing a bare coroutine, to reinforce the Part 3 connection; include a demo __main__ block covering the 3 edge cases.

parts.title: Full Contact Protocol - Capstone
parts.details: Capstone combines all prior skills. Mission control must contact a whole fleet of probes concurrently, each with its own per-probe timeout (reusing Part 2 style logic), while also enforcing an overall mission_timeout for the entire operation; if the mission_timeout expires before all probes have responded, mission control must immediately cancel every still-pending probe task to conserve emergency power and report which probes were reached versus aborted. Functions to implement: async def contact_probe(probe_id: str, delay: float, timeout: float) -> str - same behavior as Part 2 (success string or 'Lost contact with {probe_id} (timeout)' string), reimplemented here as a self-contained building block. async def run_mission(probes: list[tuple[str, float, float]], mission_timeout: float) -> dict - probes is a list of (probe_id, delay, per_probe_timeout) tuples; creates one asyncio.create_task(contact_probe(...)) per probe; wraps asyncio.gather(*tasks) in an outer asyncio.wait_for(..., timeout=mission_timeout); if it completes normally, return {'mission_status': 'success', 'results': [...]} with the list of per-probe result strings in original order; if the outer wait_for raises asyncio.TimeoutError, catch it, then for every task not yet done call task.cancel(), then await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True) to let cancellations settle without raising, and build/return {'mission_status': 'aborted', 'completed': [ids/results for tasks that finished before the abort], 'aborted': [probe_ids for tasks that were cancelled]}. Edge cases: mission_timeout generous enough for all probes to finish (full success dict), mission_timeout short enough that some probes finish and others get force-cancelled (mixed dict), all probes still pending at mission_timeout (all aborted).
parts.description_agent_notes: Present this as the season-finale style challenge tying together everything learned at Aurora Relay Station: per-probe timeouts (Part 2), manual cancellation of leftover tasks (Part 3), and automatic cancellation via an outer wait_for wrapping the whole gather call (Part 4's lesson applied at the mission level); emphasize the layered nature - individual timeouts protect against single silent probes, the mission-wide timeout protects against the whole operation dragging on too long, and cancel() is the cleanup step that stops wasted power on hopeless probes; keep tone celebratory/encouraging as the wrap-up of the problem set.
parts.coding_agent_notes: Provide starter file with: imports (asyncio), a fully given async def contact_probe (same implementation as Part 2's solution, provided directly so learner isn't re-solving it), a heavily-TODO'd async def run_mission guiding: (1) create a task per probe via asyncio.create_task(contact_probe(*probe_tuple)), (2) wrap asyncio.gather(*tasks) in asyncio.wait_for with mission_timeout inside try, (3) on success build and return the success dict from gather's results, (4) on except asyncio.TimeoutError loop tasks and cancel any not task.done(), then await asyncio.gather(*tasks, return_exceptions=True), then partition into completed vs aborted based on which tasks were cancelled vs finished, and build the aborted-status dict; include a demo __main__ block with 3 example probe lists corresponding to the three edge cases (full success, mixed, all aborted) for manual testing; comment clearly that CancelledError from gather(return_exceptions=True) will appear as exception objects in the results list and must be filtered out when building 'completed'.
